content: The criteria for implementing tuberculosis (TB) prevalence surveys, along with a list of countries meeting these criteria as of April 2022, are based on the latest available estimates of TB disease burden published by the World Health Organization (WHO). Among the 27 countries that conducted a survey between 2007 and 2021 (Category 1), 22 met the epidemiological criteria for conducting a repeat prevalence survey in April 2022. However, five countries—China, Gambia, Rwanda, Sudan, and Thailand—no longer met the criteria due to their relatively low measured levels of TB disease burden. In these countries, the focus should shift to maintaining or strengthening national notification and vital registration (VR) systems. In April 2022, there were 25 countries (Category 2) that had not previously implemented a TB prevalence survey but met the epidemiological criteria for conducting a first survey. For any country meeting the epidemiological criteria, the feasibility of conducting a survey must also be carefully assessed. According to the WHO guidelines, there are 11 prerequisites for a survey to be feasible: 1. Strong commitment and leadership from the national TB program (NTP), the Ministry of Health, and a core group of professionals. 2. Identification of a suitable institute, organization, or agency to lead and manage the survey. 3. Availability of quality-assured laboratory capacity. 4. Compliance of X-ray equipment with national regulatory authority standards. 5. Reliable and timely procurement and logistics. 6. Availability of funding. 7. Assurance of security in the field for survey teams and participants. 8. Data management conducted according to recommended standards. 9. Sufficient community participation, including in urban areas. 10. Expert review and clearance of protocols, including ethical clearance. 11. Availability of external support and technical assistance if needed. Several countries in Category 2 are likely to face challenges in meeting these feasibility criteria, particularly those implementing a survey for the first time. The epidemiological criteria for assessing whether a country should consider implementing a TB prevalence survey after 2022 include the following: For Category 1 countries (those that completed a national TB prevalence survey between 2007 and 2021): 1. An estimated prevalence of bacteriologically confirmed TB of ≥250 per 100,000 population aged ≥15 years during the previous survey. 2. More than five years since the last survey. 3. A sample size small enough (<70,000 individuals) to make surveys feasible in terms of cost and logistics. 4. A sufficient time interval between surveys to allow for a statistically meaningful comparison of prevalence. Countries meeting these criteria in April 2022 included Bangladesh, Cambodia, Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, Eswatini, Ethiopia, Ghana, India, Indonesia, Kenya, Lao People’s Democratic Republic, Lesotho, Malawi, Mongolia, Mozambique, Myanmar, Namibia, Nepal, Nigeria, Pakistan, Philippines, South Africa, Uganda, United Republic of Tanzania, Viet Nam, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. For Category 2 countries (those that did not implement a national TB prevalence survey between 2007 and 2021): 1. An estimated TB incidence of ≥150 per 100,000 population per year (all forms, all ages). 2. No nationwide VR system with standard coding of causes of death. 3. Under-5 mortality >10/1,000 live births per year. 4. A sample size small enough (<70,000 individuals) to make surveys feasible in terms of cost and logistics, considering added uncertainty due to the use of rapid molecular tests with potentially inferior performance compared to culture. 5. No reliable direct measurement of TB disease burden. 6. Indirect indicators of low access to quality health services, as defined in the WHO checklist of standards and benchmarks for TB surveillance and VR. Countries meeting these criteria in April 2022 included Afghanistan, Angola, Bhutan, Botswana, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Congo, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Djibouti, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Haiti, Kiribati, Liberia, Madagascar, Marshall Islands, Nauru, Papua New Guinea, Sierra Leone, Somalia, South Sudan, Timor-Leste, and Tuvalu. Among these, 18 countries had never implemented a national TB prevalence survey, with exceptions being Botswana, Liberia, and Sierra Leone, where surveys were conducted in the 1950s. The COVID-19 pandemic likely caused an increase in TB prevalence in countries that experienced disruptions to TB case detection, as evidenced by substantial reductions in TB case notifications. Countries that experienced major disruptions to TB diagnosis and treatment services during the pandemic may not be able to reliably detect changes in TB prevalence if they implement repeat surveys within a few years of the pandemic's onset. More generally, by the end of 2022, there was considerable uncertainty about the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on TB disease burden in many countries. For national TB prevalence surveys implemented shortly after the start of the pandemic, obtaining a new direct and precise measurement of TB prevalence is arguably a higher priority than assessing trends since the last survey, particularly in countries where major disruptions to TB case detection occurred in 2020 and/or 2021. Two diagnostic algorithms are recommended for future national TB prevalence surveys: 1. Option 1: Xpert Ultra testing of two separate sputum samples from all individuals who screen positive for TB disease, followed by confirmatory testing using liquid (MGIT) culture for all those with at least one Xpert-positive result. This option is recommended for countries that lack the capacity to ensure high-quality testing of all screen-positive individuals using liquid culture. 2. Option 2: Liquid-culture testing (MGIT) of two separate sputum samples from all individuals who screen positive for TB disease, complemented by an Xpert Ultra test to ensure that all screen-positive individuals receive a rapid result for clinical management. This option should be considered by countries with the capacity to ensure high-quality testing of all screen-positive individuals using liquid culture. Both options refer to Xpert Ultra; however, any other WHO-recommended molecular test with equivalent or better sensitivity could be used as an alternative.
